Wedding Planning

Sound Limiters at Wedding Venues: What You Need to Know

Rhona Downie · 2025-04-04 · 5 min read

Planning a wedding comes with a long list of decisions. If live music is important to you, ask your venue one question early: “Do you have a sound limiter?” Knowing the answer before you book gives your musicians time to assess the room, discuss any restrictions and recommend a suitable setup.

Originally published on 4 April 2025; restored and updated on 23 October 2026. We have refreshed the technical guidance: a decibel number alone cannot tell you whether a particular band will work in a room, and equipment changes are not a guarantee of compliance.

What is a sound limiter?

A venue sound limiter monitors or controls sound against a configured limit. Some systems reduce the audio signal; others can interrupt the power supplied to the music equipment when their trigger conditions are met. Ask which system is installed and what it controls. These are different arrangements, so “we have a limiter” is only the start of the conversation.

For examples of those different approaches, manufacturer Formula Sound describes both cut-off limiters and automatic volume-control systems.

Why do venues use them?

Ask the venue team to explain its noise requirements and how they apply to your wedding. Get the rules for the specific room, performance area and finish time in writing, and pass them to your band before you confirm the entertainment. Do not assume that arrangements at a different wedding or another room in the same building will apply to yours.

Why the decibel limit is not the whole answer

Ask for the limiter make and model, its threshold, the measurement weighting and the microphone position. Systems can use different weighting settings and internal or external microphones. Your band or sound engineer needs that context, not just a number such as “95 dB”, to assess the proposed setup.

The position of the musicians, speakers and monitoring equipment should be discussed with the venue team. Ask how long the level can exceed the threshold before the system responds, whether settings change during the evening, and who deals with a trip or reset. Do not move, cover or bypass monitoring equipment.

What can a band do about it?

Depending on the musicians, repertoire and venue requirements, options to discuss include an electronic drum kit, a quieter acoustic-drum approach, fewer onstage amplifiers, direct connections to a suitable PA, and in-ear monitoring instead of stage wedges. These are possibilities to agree with the chosen act, not equipment every band automatically supplies.

In-ear monitors can reduce the need for monitor speakers, but they do not make acoustic drums, brass, vocals or the audience silent. Likewise, connecting instruments directly to a PA does not remove the need to control the sound coming out of that PA. Ask the band what adaptations are realistic without losing the style of performance you want.

Questions to ask before booking

Does the venue have a limiter, and what type is it? What is the threshold and measurement setup? Must the band use the venue’s PA or approved technician? What equipment and stage positions are permitted? Are there restrictions on drums or brass? When must live music and recorded music finish? Can the band soundcheck before guests enter, and who is responsible for operating the system?

Choose the venue and band together

Think about the celebration you want: a relaxed acoustic set, a compact party band or a larger lineup with brass. Share that vision and the venue’s technical requirements with us early. “We have had bands before” is useful background, but it is not confirmation that every lineup will suit the same conditions.
